web_evidence.title: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold — Penguin sample
web_evidence.note: The authorized 25-page sample sustains external narration of Leamas as he, including his perceptions, memories, and thoughts, across the opening chapters.

web_evidence.title: Times Out of Joint: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
web_evidence.note: Michael Benskin's peer-reviewed Anglia article explicitly describes the novel's framework as past-tense third-person narration by an undefined, all-knowing, detached narrator, with the remainder largely dialogue.

web_evidence.title: Rereading: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold by John le Carré
web_evidence.note: William Boyd's whole-novel analysis identifies an omniscient authorial point of view that enters selected characters' thoughts and notes changes of focal character, not changes to a participating narrator.

web_evidence.title: The Spy Who Came in From the Cold Study Guide
web_evidence.note: The guide's key facts explicitly identify the novel's point of view as third-person omniscient.

search_log: Searched "The Spy Who Came in from the Cold" with "third person," "narrator," and "point of view"; found explicit whole-book descriptions in the Anglia article, Guardian analysis, LitCharts, GradeSaver, and BookRags.
Searched publisher, excerpt, first chapter, and Google Books combinations; opened Penguin's authorized sample, which provides sustained third-person prose from the opening chapters.

Searched the title with "multiple narrators," "alternating point of view," "frame narrative," "epistolary," and "diary"; found no credible indication of sustained first- or second-person base sections.
Searched specifically for narration involving Liz Gold; sources describe shifts of access or focalization between Leamas and Liz within third person, not alternating grammatical person.

The De Gruyter HTML endpoint initially returned an internal fetch error, so the full open-access Anglia article was opened through its ResearchGate publication page; an unrelated blog result was inaccessible with HTTP 429 and was not used.
person_note: The controlling voice is a nonparticipating third-person narrator. Numerous Goodreads passages sustain external narration of Leamas, Liz, and other characters while rendering their perceptions or thoughts; the authorized Penguin opening independently shows the same pattern. The scholarly whole-book analysis explicitly identifies a third-person framework, and other opened sources corroborate it. First-person and second-person forms in the quote set belong to dialogue, generic maxims, remembered speech, or authorial paratext, not autonomous base-narrative sections. Shifts between Leamas and Liz are shifts of focalization within third person, so they do not warrant ALTERNATING. Sources vary between calling the narration omniscient, objective, or limited, but that unresolved subtype does not affect the THIRD classification.
